seoTitle: Dermatologic Emergencies: Purpura, SJS/TEN, DRESS, Zoster
metaDescription: Rash in the ED, fork by fork: anaphylaxis first, non-blanching purpura and meningococcal disease, TTP and ITP, SJS/TEN and SCORTEN, DRESS, zoster, abscess.
h1: Rash and skin emergencies: the ED algorithm, fork by fork
dek: For the student on an EM, IM or dermatology rotation with a patient and a rash and a resident about to ask what is next: the first look, shock with a rash, non-blanching spots, blisters and SJS/TEN, drug rashes, vesicles and zoster, hives, abscesses, and the traps.

jumpLinks.label: Bloods for purpura and drug rashes

shortAnswer.lead: Airway, breathing and pressure before the rash.
shortAnswer.text: Anaphylaxis gets epinephrine before any skin diagnosis. Then all the skin, the conjunctivae, mouth and genitals, and every drug started in the last 8 weeks.

shortAnswer.lead: Shock with a rash: antibiotics within 1 hour.
shortAnswer.text: Blood cultures without delaying them and a fluid bolus, then the whole skin: purpura is the meningococcal route, diffuse redness the toxic shock route.

shortAnswer.lead: Non-blanching spots with fever: ceftriaxone without waiting for results.
shortAnswer.text: Blood cultures and IV ceftriaxone within 1 hour of arrival; a normal CRP or white count does not rule out meningococcal disease. No platelets before TTP is excluded, unless bleeding is major.

shortAnswer.lead: The count, film and clotting sort the purpura.
shortAnswer.text: Schistocytes with PLASMIC 6 or 7: ADAMTS13 drawn, then plasma exchange and steroids now. Isolated low platelets: ITP. Palpable purpura with normal platelets: vasculitis. A tick risk: doxycycline at any age.

shortAnswer.lead: Mucosal erosions and detaching skin: stop every suspect drug.
shortAnswer.text: SCORTEN within 24 hours and again on day 3, early transfer to a burn unit or ICU, early ophthalmology, and no prophylactic antibiotics.

shortAnswer.lead: A rash weeks after a new drug, with fever, eosinophils or organ injury, raises DRESS.
shortAnswer.text: Stop the drug and admit; moderate or severe disease gets prednisolone 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg a day, tapered over 2 to 3 months.

shortAnswer.lead: Vesicles: the host and the distribution decide.
shortAnswer.text: One dermatome, immunocompetent: oral valacyclovir 1 g three times a day within 72 hours. Nose tip: urgent ophthalmology. Disseminated or immunocompromised: IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours (20 mg/kg under 12 years).

shortAnswer.lead: Hives without anaphylaxis: a second-generation antihistamine.
shortAnswer.text: A fluctuant abscess: incision and drainage, with an antibiotic for size over 5 cm, surrounding cellulitis, a hard-to-drain site, multiple abscesses or immunosuppression.

sections.heading: What do you do first for a patient with a rash in the ED?
sections.intro: Airway, breathing and blood pressure, then the whole skin with the mucosa, and the drug history. Shock with a rash gets antibiotics within 1 hour.

sections.heading: How do you read the rash: purpura, blisters, targets, vesicles or redness?
sections.intro: The first look sorts the rash by type; the forks then read the skin in shock, the purpura bloods, the blistering pattern, the targets, the drug history and bloods, the vesicles and a hot lump.

sections.heading: How are meningococcal disease, TTP, SJS/TEN, DRESS and zoster treated?
sections.intro: Ceftriaxone with droplet precautions, doxycycline for rickettsiae, plasma exchange for TTP, steroids for adult ITP under 30, drug withdrawal and transfer for SJS/TEN, a long steroid taper for DRESS, and antivirals by host and distribution.

sections.heading: Which bloods for non-blanching spots or a drug rash?
sections.intro: Count with film, clotting, kidney and liver tests and cultures for purpura; eosinophils, atypical lymphocytes and organ tests for a widespread drug rash; urine and blood pressure for palpable purpura.

sections.heading: Blisters, targets or vesicles: what separates the diagnoses?
sections.intro: The mucosa, the Nikolsky sign, the detached area and the drug history for blisters; target shape and site for erythema multiforme against SJS; distribution and host for vesicles; isolation first for fever with a rash; fluctuance for a hot lump.

sections.heading: Where does each rash end up?
sections.intro: Every branch closes on a diagnosis and its plan, and several hand on: anaphylaxis to dyspnea, shock and necrotizing infection to sepsis and fever, cellulitis to the swollen leg pathway.

checklist.heading: SCORTEN within 24 hours, repeated on day 3

items.text: Detachment of 10% or more of body surface on day 1: 1 point.

rounds.present: 52-year-old woman with toxic epidermal necrolysis 3 weeks after starting lamotrigine: 2 days of fever and sore eyes, now painful skin coming away. Temperature 38.6, HR 128, BP 112/70. Mouth, lips, conjunctivae and genitals eroded; dusky macules with flaccid blisters, Nikolsky positive, about 35% of body surface detached, so TEN rather than SJS. SCORTEN 3: age over 40, heart rate 120 or more and detachment over 10%; BUN 18, bicarbonate 23 and glucose 130 score nothing, and there is no cancer. Plan: lamotrigine and any other suspect drug stopped and never restarted; early transfer to a burn unit or ICU; a warmed room, nonadherent dressings with the detached epidermis left in place, fluids to a MAP over 65 and urine output 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/h, opioids, early ophthalmology; skin swabs on day 1 and every 48 hours, no prophylactic antibiotics; SCORTEN again on day 3.

pimp.q: Why look in the mouth, eyes and genitals?
pimp.a: Mucosal involvement is the hallmark of SJS/TEN, present in 90% and often 1 to 3 days before the skin.

pimp.q: Petechiae and a low count. Why not transfuse platelets?
pimp.a: In TTP a platelet transfusion is contraindicated unless bleeding is major, and in HUS platelets are given sparingly.

pimp.q: Why give doxycycline to a child under 8 with possible RMSF?
pimp.a: Short courses do not cause clinically significant tooth staining, and untreated RMSF can kill 20% to 30%.

pimp.q: Why not clindamycin alone for toxic shock?
pimp.a: It suppresses toxin production but is bacteriostatic, so it is added to broad cover and never given alone.

Raised 3-zone targets, acral and symmetric, usually after an infection such as herpes simplex, are erythema multiforme; flat dusky 2-zone targets on the trunk with detachment, after a drug, are SJS. The mouth does not separate them.

pimp.q: Why not a 5-day prednisolone burst for DRESS?
pimp.a: A rapid reduction can cause severe or fatal flares and relapses; the taper runs over 2 to 3 months.

traps.text: Measuring and photographing the rash before the vital signs. Anaphylaxis and shock come first.
Holding antibiotics for a lactate, a blood count or a biopsy in shock with a rash. They go in within 1 hour.
A lumbar puncture to confirm meningococcal disease with spreading purpura. Not with extensive or rapidly spreading purpura; the throat swab, blood culture and PCR do that work.
Waiting for serology before doxycycline after a tick risk. Early serology is often negative; treat on suspicion, at any age.
Platelets before TTP is excluded, or plasma exchange held until ADAMTS13 returns. Draw the sample, then start the exchange.
IVIG first-line for an adult with ITP and platelets under 30. Corticosteroids first; IVIG joins them when a faster rise is needed.
Prophylactic antibiotics in SJS/TEN. They do not change survival; swab the skin and treat infection.
Varicella zoster immune globulin to treat chickenpox. It has no place once the rash appears.

faq.q: What do you do for a non-blanching rash with fever?
faq.a: Treat it as meningococcal disease: blood cultures and IV ceftriaxone within 1 hour of arrival, without waiting for results, because a normal CRP or white count does not rule it out. Purpura over 2 mm, a spreading rash or meningitis signs are red flags. Then the count, film, clotting and kidney tests sort ITP, TTP, HUS, DIC and vasculitis.

faq.q: What is the treatment for meningococcal disease?
faq.a: IV ceftriaxone, droplet precautions for at least 24 hours of effective antibiotics, no lumbar puncture while purpura spreads, no routine corticosteroids, and intensive care. The sources differ on the dose: StatPearls gives 2 g every 12 hours in adults in one chapter and 80 mg/kg a day in another, and NICE gives no milligram dose. Close contacts get chemoprophylaxis, such as ciprofloxacin 500 mg once in adults, rather than waiting for a fever.

Draw ADAMTS13 first, then start plasma exchange with corticosteroids without waiting for the result, with urgent hematology; caplacizumab and rituximab are considered alongside. A PLASMIC score above 5 means a high probability. No platelet transfusion unless bleeding is major. ADAMTS13 activity under 10% confirms it; over 20%, look for another cause.

A severity score for SJS/TEN, calculated within 24 hours and again on day 3: 1 point each for age over 40, heart rate 120 or more, cancer, detachment of 10% or more of the body surface, BUN over 28 mg/dL, bicarbonate under 20 and glucose over 252 mg/dL. Mortality rises from 3.2% at 0 to 1 point to 58.3% at 4.

faq.q: How do you tell SJS from TEN?
faq.a: By the detached skin as a share of body surface: SJS under 10%, SJS-TEN overlap 10% to 30%, TEN over 30%. Both come with mucosal erosions, present in 90% and often 1 to 3 days before the skin, a positive Nikolsky sign, and usually a drug started within the last 8 weeks. Both need every suspect drug stopped and early transfer.

faq.q: What is the treatment for shingles?
faq.a: In one dermatome in an immunocompetent adult: an oral antiviral within 72 hours of the rash, most effective within 48, such as valacyclovir 1 g three times a day, with analgesia. Vesicles on the nose tip mean urgent ophthalmology. Disseminated zoster or VZV on immunosuppression means admission for IV aciclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours. Systemic steroids are not routine.
